Beside this is a stone which rises no more then .15m above the group level. Beyond this is the prostrate stone measuring 2.2m by .85m which may have formed part of the row. Next is a stone .30m high, .65m wide and .65m thick. This is 2.85m from the second stone of the row. The stone at the SW is .95m from the next stone. This stone measures 1.65m high, 1.20m wide and .75m thick. The overall length of the row is 9.3m.

KE010-017----:
The site comprises an almost circular area enclosed by a ditch bank and internal fosse and has a well-defined entrance feature. The site has external dimensions of 77.7m SE-NW and 74.9m NE-SW. A small portion of the NW of the monument is destroyed and cut off by a modern roadway, fieldbanks and a drainage ditch. The portion of the site in the NW field has been levelled and is today noticeable only by slight variations in vegetation, which presumably mark the one-time presence of the bank and internal fosse. Examination of the site's features are by necessity limited to the much larger portion of the site in the SE field.
There is a quite pronounced outer ditch in the NE and SW sectors, but it does not appear clearly about the rest of the site. It varies in width between 1.8m and 4.2m and appears as a clearly defined if shallow depression enclosing the site. In the NE its deepest point is .45m below ground level and 1.45m below the top of the bank; in the SW it is .35m below ground level and 1.3m below the top of the bank. It is probable however that this ditch is not contemporaneous with the rest of the site. At the sectors where the ditch appears the bank has a terraced effect at its top and it is significant that this effect does not appear where the bank is not enclosed by the ditch; in all likelihood the field-builders augmented the height of the bank with material dug from the ditch.
Apart from the destroyed portion of the site in the NW field, the bank is well preserved, high and wide. Excepting the sectors enclosed by the outer ditch, it is flat-topped. Where it is enclosed by the ditch there appears, as mentioned above, to be a more terraced effect. It ranges in width between 6.6m and 10.9m. At the NE sector it measures 1.4m above the outer ditch and 1.4m above the internal fosse. In the SW sector the picture is similar, where the bank measures 1.3m above the outer ditch and 1.1m above the internal fosse.
The internal fosse is well-defined. It ranges in width between 6m-11.8m. In the SW sector its greatest depth is 1.1m below the top of the bank and .8m below the site's internal area. In the NE sector its greatest depth is 1.2m below the top of the bank and .8m below the interior.
The entrance is a clearly defined gap 9.7m in width in the bank and internal fosse, allowing unimpeded entrance through the ESE. The interior of the site is somewhat higher in level than the surrounding farmland. The surface is uneven, but there are no surviving traces of archaeological features above ground level. It has dimensions of 40.4m (SE-NW) and 38m (NE-SW); the former dimension however does not take into account the portion destroyed at the NW of the site (Paddy O'Donovan, NMAJ 1985, 75-77).
The above description is derived from C. Toal, ‘North Kerry Archaeological Survey’. Dingle. Brandon in association with FAS Training and Employment Authority (1995), no. 99. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 2 August 2013

Located in a small field or paddock in front of a series of buildings, including a dwelling house and sheds, on the S side of a large rounded hill. The dominant aspect id to the S, but there are good views also to the E and W.
This is an impressive standing stone, known locally as ‘Carriglea’. It is triangular in shape, measuring 1.5m in height, 1.6m in maximum width and 0.5m thick, and aligned E-W on its long axis. The type of stone is uncertain, but it appears to be a form of granite. It was formerly incorporated into a small field boundary. This must be in the recent past, as there is no settlement indicated here on the Ordnance Survey 1st edition map, or on the subsequent 25 inch map. The stone is marked as ‘Carriglea’ on both these maps.

KE020-020001-:
This stone is marked on the 1842 and 1897 OS maps as 'Gallaun'. Rising to a height of 2.2m with a peak at the top, originally it lay on top of a mound but was removed to a fieldbank about 20.4m N in the 1940s (KE020-020004-).
Standing stone within possible ring-barrow (KE020-020002-) described by Lynch (1892, 80-3) as follows; 'Mr. B. M'Elligott, a farmer in that neighbourhood, was employed with some workmen in widening the old road which passes near the gallaun [KE020-020001-]. In the course of his work, within about 3 feet [0.9m] of the rut of the old road, and about 2 feet [0.6m] below the surface, he found some small and thin flags of limestone, on removing which he found they covered a grave or tomb [KE020-020003-) lined at the sides with flags of the same kind as those covering it. The grave lay within about 80 yards of the conspicuous gallaun or pillar stone [KE020-020001-] which crowns the highest point of the limestone ridge that runs east and west for some miles through the plains of Clanmaurice.  The townland around the gallaun is known as Ardconnel (the height of Conal), and I have no doubt that this Ardconnel is the very ancient Ardconail mentioned in the "Book of Rights" as the site of one of the Portaibh or Royal seats of the Kings of Cashel.
This pillar stone, which is a very remarkable one, visible from every point of the compass for many miles, consists of a block of whinstone, 8 feet [2.4m] high over the present surface, about 3 feet [0.9m] broad, and 15 inches [0.4m] thick, must have been brought from the cliffs near Kerry Head, about 9 miles distant, where stones of that kind are found in large quantities. This may have been the monumental stone of the illustrious chief Conal, whose name is thus preserved by the townland designation, but of whose name and fame history and legend are silent. The gallaun is surrounded by a shallow trench and embankment forming a circle [KE020-020002-] about 40 yards [36m] in diameter. "Within about 13 perches [65m] west of the gallaun on the same ridge are the remains of what must have been a large and strong Cashel or Cahir, called Cahirfert [KE020-037----]'.
Revised by: Caimin O'Brien

KE030-028----:
'This 2.10m tall, irregularly shaped standing stone is situated immediately to the north-west of a bi-vallate ringfort (KE030-029----) in a field which is used for grazing. This field is bounded to the west and south by the River Lee, and the surrounding land contains areas of limestone outcrop. This red sandstone gallaun is aligned NNW/SSE, rectangular at base where it measures 0.50m by 0.35, bulges out slightly about 1.0m above the ground to 0.60m by 0.40m, before tapering to a point. A 10cm wide, 2cm deep band has been worn into the stone c.0.20m from the base, although no pock marks are evident. Two hollows occur on the north face of the stone, 8cm and 4cm wide respectively, and both 2cm deep. These are natural solution hollows. This stone stands on the western limits of a low mound. The survey carried out by the Irish Tourism Association in 1944-45 (MS copy Kerry County Library) describes the fort at Lissooleen (KE030-029----) as two ringed with a north facing entrance. It also note that outside the entrance there is a tall slender  "gallaun" 8feet high and that 2 feet above the ground a ring has been worn in the stone.'
Description from ‘The Prehistoric Settlement of the Lee Valley, Tralee, Co. Kerry; A Landscape Perspective’ by Michael Connolly. PhD Thesis UCC 2008

A stone alignment situated on the lower E slopes of Brandon mountain, commanding an extensive view across Brandon Bay towards the central mountain ridge that forms the backbone of the Dingle Peninsula. Three stones, standing in a WSW-ENE line, are orientated on the rising sun at the summer solstice (Lynch 1981b, 26); 2 others lie prostrate and partly buried 2.15m and c. 6.3m to W. These latter had already fallen by the early 19th century as, though 5 stones are shown on the 1st edition of the OS map, only the 3 standing stones are described in the OSNB (Cloghane, 25). Positioned 1.6m and 1.7m apart, the stones stand 2.75m, 2.14m and 2.1m high, the decrease in height from E-W being accentuated by a gentle drop in ground level in the same direction. The 4th prostrate slab measures 1.9m x 1.7m; the 5th, partly buried and obscured by vegetation, measures 2.35m x at least 1.55m, and is not noted in any previous accounts. Macalister (1945, 170) appears to be correct in dismissing Ferguson's account (1887, 48-9) of indecipherable ogham scores on the 2nd stone.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 52. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE035-072001-:
The available information regarding the precise location and classification of this site is confused. On the 1st edition of the OS map it was shown as a line of 2 standing stones (KE035-072001-) and a small rectangular building (KE035-072----) and it was named 'Cloghauns'. On the 2nd edition, a circular structure, named 'Cloghauns' was marked about 20-30m SE of the position on the 1st edition. There is now no trace of either clochaun or standing stones at the site which lies in rough wet pastureland on the SE slopes of the Owenmore valley.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 1571. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 6 August 2013
KE035-073001-:
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
Cuppage (1986, 20-6, no. 25 (a)) records that 'three of the stones of the gallery bear rock art designs.' These designs include a single cup-and-circle, twelve shallow cup-marks, two possible cup-marks and a penannular circle. These are shown in Cuppage (ibid., fig. 13b). The 'Gallaun' indicated on the 1st and 2nd ed. OS 6-inch maps to the SW of this wedge tomb is probably the one that is noted by Cuppage (ibid.) as a 'single outer-wall stone [which] stands at the W end of the S side [of the wedge tomb]'; this is also noted by O'Nuallain (1982, 55, fig. 20).
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
Date of upload: 6 January 2012

KE036-002----:
Located on low-lying level ground at the base of the Magharees Peninsula, about 1/2 mile south of Lough Gill. This standing stone, 2m long, .5m to .8m wide and from .25 to .8m thick, was knocked over about 10 years ago (local information). It now lies against the field wall immediately S of its original position.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 119. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE036-009----:

A 'Gallaun' was marked on the OS maps on the N slopes of Corrin hill, overlooking Tralee Bay and the adjacent coastal plain. The rough, marshy land in which it stood has recently been reclaimed and there is no trace of the stone.

KE036-041----:
This stone alignment is located on the low-lying level strip of land between the Slieve Mish mountains and Tralee Bay. It consists of 3 stones orientated ENE-WSW, the easternmost now split vertically into 3 separate portions, and the westernmost lying prostrate. The latter, measuring 3.22m x 1.3m x .38m, would have been the tallest stone, its nearest neighbour, 2m to E, being 2.76m high and measuring 1m x .75m at base. The 3rd stone stands 2.2m to E again and would originally have measured 1 to 1.2m x c. 0.7m at base. Two portions are 2.17m and 2m high respectively, while the 3rd fragment is only .45m high.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 51. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 108. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE037-035----:
The precise details of this site are a little uncertain. Situated on the steep E side of Glenfais, with extensive views along the valley and N across Tralee Bay, it is shown on the OS maps as a single 'Gallaun'. However, it was later described as 'an alignment of 3 stones' orientated roughly N-S (Browne et al. 1911, 49). The two N stones, 2.7m and 3.4m long, lay prostrate 3.4m apart; the 3rd stone stood 7.7m to S and was 2.5m high and 1.98m wide tapering to a point at top. The number of prostrate slabs was elsewhere (CKFC 1939, 19 and 1941, 181) given as 3 and 7 or 8. The stones had been broken up and removed by 1945 (CKFC 1945, 576).
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 54. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE037-042----:
The 'Gallaun' marked on the OS map now lies prostrate on the fairly level tract of land between the Finglas river and the foot of Corrin hill. It has broken into at least 3 fragments, the largest measuring 2.3m x 1.5m x .2m. Windele (1838, 106) described it as 3.7m high and 1.5m wide. The measurements in the OSNB (Kilgobban, 34) are slightly less: 3m high and 1.2m in diameter.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 122. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE038-003004-:
'The Ordnance Survey 1st and 2nd Edition 6" maps record "Gallauns" at this location. No trace of the stones now remains, though a large red sandstone monolith uncovered during dredging along the shore in 1996 is very probably one of the stones. This stone is 3.75m in overall length and measures 1.3m by 0.9m at base. Local information suggests that the stones were extant up until the 1930's and that there were three of them - two close together and a third some 20m to the north-east. This would suggest a stone pair or partially extant alignment and a single standing stone. The possibility that the single stone had been moved at some time prior to the 1930's, from an original position close to the other two, was suggested by the landowner. The minutes of the County Kerry Field Club for a meeting in November 1940 state that: Lying on the beach outside this gateway (that leading from Annagh Church) is a massive gallaun of red sandstone almost completely buried in the clay.'
Description from ‘The Prehistoric Settlement of the Lee Valley, Tralee, Co. Kerry; A Landscape Perspective’ by Michael Connolly. PhD Thesis UCC 2008
Date of upload: 20 June 2012
KE038-003007-:
'These stones were marked on the second edition of the OS map as Gallauns-site of. A search of the field in which they were marked revealed that they were, in fact, removed during clearance of the field and deposited beside the field boundary. These stones are of red sandstone, and are very noticeable as they occur in an area of limestone. They comprise of two complete rectilinear boulders and a third one which is now split and lies in two pieces immediately to the north. All the stones are rectangular in section. The largest is 2.63m in length, 0.90m in width and 0.38m thick. The middle one is 1.25m in length, 0.55m in width and 0.45m thick. The smallest stone lies in two pieces as stated above. The larger of the two fragments measures 0.60m in length, 0.90m in width and 0.30m thick. The smaller fragment measures 0.22m in length, 0.40m in width and 0.20m thick. This in effect gives a total length of 0.82m for the third stone. All the boulders tapered slightly towards the top. As the stones decreased/increased in height in a uniform way from largest to smallest. It is most likely that this is, in fact, the remains of a three-stone alignment.'  O'Donovan (1841) recorded a stone fort (Tonakilla Fort KE038-003005-) east of the church at Annagh [KE038-003001-]. He also noted that at the south-east side of the caher there were eight stones, six of which are laid prostrate, and two are standing upright, and placed as if forming the "head and foot of a grave, at a distance of 10 feet asunder". This description was subsequently quoted by Borlase (1875,5).  Cross reference with KE037-049----
Compiled by Michael Connolly for the Archaeological Survey of Ireland as part of a survey of the Lee Valley area in 1996-97.
Date of upload: 23 May 2012
KE038-010004-:
Fort (KE038-010003-) and possible standing stone described by Hitchcock (1854-5) as follows; 'The few portions of bones which I send were picked up by myself in underground chamber discovered, towards the end of June last, on the Messrs. Hilliard's at Ballydunlea, near Tralee. As this was evidently the first time the souterrain (KE038-010001-) had been disturbed since its desertion by the original occupants, perhaps I may be permitted to give some account of it. The 'cave' was discovered in the course of digging up an old stone fence which ran down through the length of the field. There is no trace of a fort on the surface; but a mound like a portion of tumulus [KE038-010002-] is to be seen, overgrown with blackthorn, briers, &c. This mound may have formed part of the embankment of fort; but it is now difficult to ascertain this, as it seems to have lost much of its original form, and no further trace of a fort remains. The entrance to the cave is from the west side, where we get into a long passage, which slopes down deeper till it reaches the level of the door of the inner chamber. The entrance passage and chamber lie nearly east and west, and as the old fence lay in the same direction, it must have passed over them. I could see no trace of an inscription on any of the lintels in this souterrain. In the adjoining field, and nearer to the river, there is what I always considered an interesting fort [KE038-010003-].  It is formed of small stones, I believe rather a rare occurrence and in the centre is a large and rude stone [KE038-010004-], placed in an oblique position, as if it had served the purpose of an altar for sacrifice.  I have often sat on this stone, meditating on its probable use, and on the curious fort in which it is situated'.
See field inspection report (diary NF7, 189-90) (SMR file). According to the report, the original location of this possible standing stone was at the centre of the cashel (KE038-010003-). The landowner informed the fieldworker that stone is still here but is now buried.
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien
Date of upload: 28 January 2022

KE038-074----:
Excavations of a Hilltop enclosure (KE038-022----) and passage tomb by Michael Connolly under licence No. 96E0138 was summarised as follows; 'During the summer of 1996 excavations in the townland of Ballycarty, 4km east of Tralee, Co. Kerry, revealed the presence of a complex and unusual archaeological landscape on and around a 200m-long limestone spur, 50m south of the River Lee The excavations were necessitated by the construction of a new link between the existing Killarney Road and Tralee town (the N22), and, while an enclosure had been centrally recorded on the spur, survey showed the spur to have a far more complex history.
The passage tomb
The area of excavation was on the very western tip of the spur, where, prior to sod-stripping, only a very low undulation of the ground surface was visible. Removal of the sod from this area revealed that the mound was in fact a low stone and earthen cairn with a central 0. 17m-deep depression on its surface. Sod-stripping also revealed the presence of a very collapsed stone rampart which abutted the cairn on its southern side and ran across the western end of the spur.
Excavation revealed that the cairn was laid down in alternating layers of stone and earth and covered a small passage tomb. The tomb consisted of three concentric rings of lime. stone boulders, cut by a roughly built passage, 1.4m long, on their western side. The stone rings were excellently preserved in the southern half of the site but had been substantially destroyed in the northern half by the construction of a later stone and earth bank, probably associated with the rampart.
The western side of the site also revealed the presence of a well-constructed curved monumental façade. The fa9ade was built of limestone slabs, two courses high in some places, and remained to a height of 1.3m. It had been added to the site during a second phase of activity which saw the construction of a slab and boulder orthostatic passage, c. 3m long, through the façade. This passage led to a subrecrangular rock-cut chamber which may originally have been walled with orthostats, later removed. The chamber measured 1.5m x l.2m.
In a final phase of activity at the site, the front (more westerly) half of this Phase 2 passage was restructured and realigned through the addition of a wedge-shaped section of drystone walling to the existing southern side wall and the construction of a completely new drystone section of the northern side wall. Interestingly, the interface between the two differing construction techniques of the extant passage— drystone walling in the outer, more westerly portion and orthostatic construction in the portion nearest the chamber— is marked by the only surviving lintel. The lintel appears to have rolled off two stones which overhang the passage immediately inside (east of) its current position, and indicates a height for the passage at this point of 0.67m.
Also during this final phase the existing chamber was replaced by a D-shaped drystone-built chamber, which was placed inside the existing rock-cut feature. This chamber produced a quantity of cremated bone and some worked flints. …

Standing stone described by O'Hare (1996, 11) as follows; 'This sandstone block, which is roughly rectangular in section, stands in an area of mountainous bog, on a break in a west facing slope. Standing in a slight depression, the base of the stone was at the time of this visit, concealed to a height of 40cm by water. KE042-027----: Cow and Thief's Stone described by Cuppage (1986, 323, no. 855) as follows; 'These are 2 stones set on either side of the roadway about 150m S of the graveyard [KE042-026017-]. The E stone stands 0.81m high at the base of the road boundary fence but the W stone is now buried. Legend tells of a thief who attempted to steal a cow but was prevented from doing so by a holy man who caused the thief's foot to stick in one stone and the cow's hoof to become embedded in the other (Curran no.8). It is not clear what the original purpose of these stones was or what, if any, was their relationship to the ecclesiastical site'.

KE042-044----:
This structure, located on the low-lying level land S of Smerwick Harbour, was removed about 40 years ago. The only visible remains consist of an irregular area, 10m x 4m, raised slightly above the surrounding field level. Westropp (1910, 203) described the feature as a 'dolmen', comprised of 3 roughly rectangular chambers partly embedded in a low mound. The contiguous but irregularly-positioned chambers were defined by large slabs, up to 8 feet (c. 2.4m) long, but no heights were recorded. Internally the chambers measured c. 8 foot 10 inches (c. 2.7m) x 4 feet (c. 1.2m), c. 4 foot 2 inches (c. 1.3m) x c. 7 feet 6 inches (c. 2.3m) and 5 feet 2 inches (c. 1.6m) x 4 feet 2 inches (c. 1.3m). The largest chamber was roofed by 2 large slabs, the others by a single slab each. The 2 larger chambers were aligned NE-SW but did not form a straight line. The W chamber was set slightly further S than the E one, and the angle formed between the two at S was occupied by the smallest chamber. From the description and plan provided by Westropp, it is not possible to classify this monument with certainty. It may have consisted of a group of cist-graves or of an unclassified megalithic tomb.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 37. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 3 August 2013
This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 6/1932).

The taller SE stone is 1.9m high, 1.1m wide and a maximum of .3m thick. A large packing stone is exposed at the base. The NW stone is 1.6m high and .9m x .4m at base.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 66. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE042-066----:
A standing stone now located within a farmyard on a gentle slope between Reenconnell to W and the lowlying land surrounding Smerwick Harbour to E and S. It stands 2.8m high and is 1.24m wide terminating in a rounded point at top; NE-SW. The E elevation is almost totally concealed by a stack of concrete blocks. A single packing stone is visible at the W end of the NW side.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 87. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE042-067----:
On the lower slopes of Reenconnell, about 30m W of an impressive ringfort (KE042-069----) and 150m W of the 'Saint's Road' (KE034-112001-), is a stone standing 1.53m high and measuring c. 0.52m in width and only .11 to .17m in thickness, its long axis orientated 10 degrees E of N. KE042-142----:
Labbanirweeny/Leaba an Fhir Mhuimhnigh: Located on fairly level ground near the summit of Caherard Hill, this well-preserved wedge-tomb commands an extensive outlook stretching from Brandon mountain in the NE, to the mountains of the Iveragh peninsula in the S, to Mount Eagle and Croaghmarhin in the W.
The structure consists of a slightly wedge-shaped gallery, covered by 3 overlapping roofstones and flanked at either side by the remains of an outer-wall. It is surrounded by vague traces of a low mound rising no more than .25m above ground level. The gallery measures 4m in overall length and is aligned E-W. It is 1.2m wide at the open W end and 1.1m wide at the E end. It decreases in height from 1m at the entrance to .6m at the backstone.
Two low stones at the W end of the gallery are set immediately inside the lines of the N and S walls and seem to represent the sides of a short, narrow portico. The side-walls of the main gallery are each formed by 5 orthostats and decrease in height from W to E. The westernmost stone on the S side has collapsed and consequently the W roofstone now lies in a tilted position. The E end of the gallery is closed by a single slab. Two stones outside the S wall and a single stone outside the N wall form a doubling of the side-walls. A 2nd stone outside the N wall may be a buttress. Three outer-wall stones are present on either side of the gallery and the 2 easternmost extend slightly beyond the E end of the tomb.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 33. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
Date of upload: 3 August 2013
KE042-149----:
The precise location of a possible wedge tomb located on top of Ballyferriter Hill that was recorded as destroyed prior to 1852 (Hitchcock 1852, 137) was recently identified by local archaeologist Billy Mag Fhloinn.  Situated in upland area,  on top of high ridge running roughly NE-SW which forms the townland boundary with Ballyferriter.  Extensive views from W through N to E, overlooking the villahe of Ballyferriter and Ferriter’s Cove to NW and Smerwick Harbour to NE.  The hill of Cruach Mhárthain is visible 1.2km away at the SW end of the ridge with Cnoc an Phréacháin 350m away at the E end of the ridge.
The monument classification as a wedge-tomb (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 56) is based on an engraving published by Chatterton (1839, 201). In 1838 the monument was mentioned by Lady Chatterton in her Rambles in the South of Ireland, where it was described as located on Ballyferriter Hill, and being ‘a very curious piece of antiquity, once an altar supposed to have been used for offering sacrifices to the sun’.  In 1852 Hitchcock wrote the following account about the monument; 'I have found in lady Chatterton's very interesting Rambles in the South of Ireland, second edition, vol. i. p. 189, an engraving of a cromleac on Ballyferriter hill, which may probably be added to the number already mentioned; but I regret to say that this cromleac, or, as lady Chatterton calls it, "sun altar," does not now exist, the stones which composed it having been broken and carried away for building purposes, as if there were no others in the neighbourhood!'.
Local archaeologist, Billy Mag Fhloinn recorded that the name; 'Altóir na Gréine, meaning Altar of the Sun, also appears in local tradition from the Schools Folklore Collection in 1939, where it was mentioned as a place where mass was said during Penal Times. It is included in a list of placenames and accounts relating priests celebrating clandestine masses at remote locations, offering a clue as to where the idea of it being an altar came from:  Tá Altóir na Gréine lastuas do Bhaile'n Fhirtéuraig Thiar. Bhíodh Aifreann á léigheamh annso leis. Sé fáth go dtugadh an ainm seo air, ná nuair a dh'eirigheadh an ghrian thoir thaithnigheadh sí ar seo (The Altar of the Sun is above Ballyferriter West. Mass was read here also. The reason it is so-called is when the sun rose in the east it would shine on this place). Another potential name for the monument may be Púicín Bhriain, which is mentioned in a local song as part of a series of placenames traced by a local farmer in pursuit of a lost cow.  Its location between Slighe-na-Naomh and Cathar Léith fits the current site, and would be passed on the track over the mountain from Márthain to Baile an Fheirtéaraigh. That a wedge tomb might be referred to as a púicín (meaning a poke for shutting in lambs) is evidenced from the example at Dún Meánach, 25 km east near Lispole, which was known as Púicín an Chairn'.
Billy Mag Fhloinn recorded the presence of three slabs in close proximity to each other, one standing upright. The latter matches the general shape of one of the orthostats supporting the roof slab in Chatterton’s illustration. …

This pair of standing stones is the northernmost element in a complex of megalithic monuments which are grouped at the SE end of the townland of Milltown (formerly Kilbrack), less than 1/2km W of where the Milltown river flows into Dingle Harbour. About 50m to S are 2 large recumbent stones (KE043-214----), one of which bears a variety of rock art motifs on its upper surface. Gallán na Cille Brice (KE043-215----) stands about 30m further to SW, and on the S side of the main road, c. 250m SSW again, is another standing stone (KE053-004----). Macalister (1898b, 164) reports that 'at least one other gallán was destroyed in this district when the present road was made in 1822'.
Up until recently the pair of standing stones stood 1.4m apart in a NE-SW line; the NE stone now lies prostrate. Prior to its collapse, it stood 2.2m high and measured 1.5m x .6m at base (Ó Nualláin 1978b, 67). The SW stone, now .79m high, was 1.5m high in 1898 (Macalister, 161), and appears to have broken across the top. A loose stone, lying beside it and measuring 1m long x .22m high, is probably the missing fragment. Known locally as Geataí na Glóire (the Gates of Glory or Paradise).
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 64. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Triangular-shaped standing stone immediately to N of townland boundary with BAILE RISTÍN (Ballyrishteen), on  poorly drained mountainous region with commanding views to N.  Standing stone identified by Ina Doyle, not depicted on any edition of the OSi historic maps.

KE044-011----:
The 'Gallaun' marked on the OS maps, c. 450m SW of KE044-013----, no longer survives. It was '7 feet (2.1m) high'(OSM). At approximately the same location there is a long, low and densely overgrown mound of earth and stones, with several large, possible kerb stones along the perimeter. It measures at least 14m E-W, and is 10m wide and .8m high at the W end decreasing in both width and height towards the E. A depression is visible on the upper surface. The small cairn of stones to SW of its W end may simply be the result of field clearance.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 149. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

It measures 1.31m x .75m at base; ENE-WSW. A prostrate slab, 3.6m long N-S, 1.15m wide and at least .8m thick, lies 2.5m to E but may formerly have stood upright.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 59. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

The larger stone measures 1.83m in height, 1.95m in maximum width and c. 0.3m in thickness. The smaller stone stands .75m to E and is 1.6m high (1.8m high on S side where peat has been removed), 1.18m wide and .23m thick. A stone bearing cup-and-circle designs was located c. 150m to W in the adjoining townland (KE044-026----).

KE045-010----:
Situated on the fairly steep lower slopes of Knockbeg, overlooking the Emlagh river valley to S, is a standing stone known as 'An Galláinín' (An Seabhac 1939, 287). Almost square in plan at base and roughly rectangular in elevation, it leans heavily to S but would stand 1.9m high if erect; it measures .41m x .4m at base. A few cms from its WNW side, a 2nd stone is set on edge in the ground. This measures .95m N-S x .2m x .42m high. Several small packing stones are also visible. An Seabhac refers to a large prostrate stone in the adjacent field known as 'Páircín na Cloiche'; this was not located and its archaeological significance is not known.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 109. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE045-013001-:
Marked 'Cromlech' on the OS maps and referred to as An Cromleac by An Seabhac (1939, 288), this is the westernmost tomb of the group. It stands about 45m W of tomb 2 and about 100m SW of tomb 3. The structure consists of a wedge-shaped gallery covered, at its E end, by a single roofstone. The gallery sides are each formed of 2 stones. The westernmost stones on either side are tall and well-matched and are set outside the ends of the adjoining sidestones. The tops of both stones slope downwards from W to E. A single stone closes the gallery at its E end. Immediately outside the E stone on the N side is another slab which forms a doubling of the gallery wall. Two outer-wall stones are present to S of the gallery. A transverse stone beyond the W end of the gallery is probably a septal-or sill-stone. A loose, prostrate stone lies between this and the end of the gallery. The gallery measures 3m long or 3.75m long from the septal-stone. It is 1.4m wide at W, 1.6m near the middle and 1.45m at the backstone. The levels of the sidestones indicate a sharp decrease in height from W to E. There are traces of a mound to W and N of the structure but a drain curves around the W end of this and its outline here cannot be original.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 35, Tomb1. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (No. 5/1970).
Date of upload: 6 August 2013
KE045-013002-:
This lies about 45m E of tomb 1 and is deeply buried in peat. It is filled with water and was consequently difficult to examine. The edges of 2 roofstones protrude from the peat and beneath these is a sharply wedge-shaped chamber. At the N is a sidestone at least 2.2m long, and set inside the E end of this is a 2nd stone, .5m long. The top of an orthostat, 1.5m long, is exposed on the opposite side of the gallery. The edges of a few more stones are exposed in the gallery area but the function of these is not known. Two stones protrude from the bog beyond the W end of the gallery. Though the monument is largely concealed in the bog the visible remains are sufficient to allow classification as a wedge-tomb.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 35, Tomb 2. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
This monument, subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (No. 5/1970), was removed in 1981.
Revised by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 3 October 2016
KE045-013003-:
The northernmost tomb, named Altar/An Althóir, consists of the ruins of a gallery flanked at either side by an outer-wall. The gallery appears to have been about 5m in overall length and is divided into 3 sections. A short portico at the W is separated from the main chamber by a large septal-stone which protrudes beyond the gallery walls at either side. The portico is about 1m long and was probably about .9m wide but the N side is missing. The S side consists of a single slab and this is linked to the outer-wall by a facade stone. The main chamber consists of 2 elements, differentiated from each other by a pair of transverse stones set into the gallery walls. The front section is 1.2m long and .8m wide and the side walls are each formed by a single slab. The S wall is doubled. The E section of the main chamber is .9m wide but the E end is missing. The N side consists of 3 stones and the S of two. On the N side, 3 stones form a doubling of the gallery wall. The levels of the sidestones of the tomb indicate a general decrease in height from W to E, and the E section narrows slightly towards the back. The outer-wall on either side is represented by 4 stones, those on the S side converging sharply on the E end of the gallery. A shallow curved depression is visible in the ground beyond the W end of the tomb. A prostrate stone, 1.6m in maximum dimension, lies to the S of the front of the tomb. This apparently bears a number of cup-marks (CKFC 1939, 53; Sheehy 1982, 32).
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 35, Tomb 3. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (No. 5/1970).
Date of upload: 6 August 2013

A single upright stone (KE045-013007-) is located a further 11m to NE.
Compiled by: Alison McQueen and Vera Rahilly
Date of upload: 11 January 2017
KE045-013007-:

Compiled by: Alison McQueen and Vera Rahilly
Date of upload: 11 January 2017

A standing stone situated on the lower S slopes of the central mountain ridge, overlooking the Anascaul valley to S and the narrow valley that lies N of Flemingstown mountain to E. It is trapezoidal in plan at base, the sides measuring .6m, .8m, .52m and .8m. They taper slightly towards the top where, at 2.5m above the ground, the stone measures .4m x .1m. About 400m further uphill to N are 2 boulders decorated with rock art motifs (KE045-003----).
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 81. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

A standing stone, cup-marked stone and possible cist (KE045-082----) are grouped in close proximity to one another, overlooking the Anascaul valley from the level summit of a local E-W rise, in generally undulating pastureland at the foot of Knockafeehane. The standing stone measures 1.24m x .65m at base, the sides rising irregularly to a pointed top at a height of 3.25m; E-W. A simple Latin cross with expanded terminals has been added to the N face about 1.25m from the base.

This stone stands on the crest of a low hill located centrally in the Emlagh river valley, immediately N of the gap in the coastal mountain ridge through which the river flows towards Castlemaine Harbour. It is now incorporated into an E-W field wall which obscures the lower portion of its N face. It is 2.65m high, c. 1m wide and .6m thick; NE-SW. A Latin cross with expanded terminals has been carved on the N face. On the 2nd edition of the OS map a standing stone is also shown untitled c. 50m to WNW; it does not survive.

KE047-026----:
Listed in the RMP for Co. Kerry as an Enclosure, there is however no evidence or references in the paper file to the existence of an enclosure at this location.  Therefore the classification has been changed from Enclosure to Standing Stone as this monument was not listed in the Kerry RMP. The Ardcanaght (Aird Chánachta/Hill of the Tribute) Stone, in the parish of Kilgarrylander (Cill Gharraí an Lóndraigh), barony of Trughanacmy (Triúcha an Aicme), Co. Kerry. National Monument Number 430.  In improved pasture (20m OD), on a very gentle E-facing slope of low lying ground in the River Maine valley. Excellent views of the MacGillycuddy Reeks to S and Slieve Mish mountains to N.  A smooth and fractured standing stone (dims. H 1.62m; L 0.95m; Wth 0.87m) with decorated surface (dims. H 1.55m; Wth 0.66m) bearing extremely faint and weathered rock art upon the ENE face. Very faint traces of approximately five cup-and-one-ring motifs (average diam. 15cm; ring Wth 4cm; D 3mm; cup diam. 5cm; D 4mm) are barely traceable upon lower part of this elevation. Three single ring elements and two two-ring elements may represent the remains of deeply weathered cup-and-ring or cup-and-two ring motifs. Known as the Ardcanaght Stone. A rectangular area (dims. 3.5m N-S; 3.5m E-W) around the monument is enclosed by a steel fence, separating it from rest of field. Three fragments of ogham stones (KE047-026001-/003-) within the railed enclosure, at base of standing stone. 3D model of standing stone decorated with cup-and-ring motifs visible at https://skfb.ly/pBxxq
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien based on details provided by Alison McQueen and Vera Rahilly
KE047-052----:
Situated on N facing slope on S side of the broad valley of the River Maine. The monument is aligned N-S with the entrance facing downslope to N. Remains comprise two portal stones and a roofstone. The portals stand 0.90m apart and both lean markedly to the E. The W portal measures 1.20m long, is 0.40m wide at the top narrowing to c. 0.30m at the base, and, if erect, would be 1.60m high. The E portal is 1.80m in maximum length, 0.60m thick and, if erect, would be 1.70m high. The E portal rests against an upright stone (0.60m long, 0.22m thick, and 0.35m H) but it is unclear whether or not it originally formed part of the structure as it may have been part of a field fence that formerly abutted the monument here (see below). The roofstone measures 3.75m long, 2.60m wide and 0.80m thick. It is clearly displaced and rests on the E portal. Its S end rests on the ground above a stone (0.80m long, 0.15m thick, and in excess of 0.30m in depth) whose exposed edge is visible beneath it within the chamber. A split boulder slab (1.15m x 1.10m x 0.27m thick) lies in the chamber area and was moved to its present position from the rear of the chamber (pers comm. landowner). It is impossible to know if it ever formed part of the tomb structure proper. The exact dimensions of the chamber cannot be ascertained with certainty but it would have been c. 2m long measuring from the interior edges of the portal stones to where the roofstone rests on the ground. A drawing of the tomb by Commander O'Connel (March 1939, SMR file) shows the monument incorporated within a field fence which abutted the S end of the roofstone and the E face of the E portal stone. This fence was removed in early 1993 leaving a low mound of earth and stone around the monument's E side. Other than that, there is no evidence of a surrounding cairn or mound. The monument is undergoing excavation and conservation (license number 15E0103).

KE047-059----:
Situated on a level shoulder on a gentle slope within Killacloghane Wood, the remains consist of a group of prostrate slabs within an apparently hollowed-out area. A large roofstone-like slab (3.10m by 2.40m; 0.50m think) aligned N–S is partly overlapped by a smaller second slab at the N (1.85m E–W) which appears to have been broken off. Beneath the larger slab on its W side are two partly-overlapping slabs which may be interpreted as fallen portal stones. The S slab measures at least 1.10m wide, is over 0.45m thick and, if erect, would have been c. 2.15m. The N slab rests on and partly overlaps the W side of the previous slab: it measures 1.05m wide, 0.25m thick and, if erect, would have been over 1.70m. While the remains cannot be classified with any degree of certainty, comparison with the nearby portal tomb in the same townland c. 1km to the WSW (KE047-052----) would suggest that interpretation as a possible portal tomb would not be inconsistent with the evidence; this, however, is purely tentative and a full elucidation of the monument must await further investigation.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 19 October 2015

KE049-028001-:
Stone circle described by O'Hare (1996, 11-12) as follows; 'Four stones, three upright and one fallen, are visible at this site, enclosing a roughly horseshoe shaped area which lies open to the north. A fifth stone standing to the southwest, appears to form an outlier. The stones are standing on a level break in a steep southeast facing slope, in an area of rough mountain pasture.  The site commands a view over the roiling land which lies to the east, southeast, south and southeast.  Beginning at east and running clockwise, the dimensions of each stone are as follows: Stone 1 measures 1.05m in height, 56cm in breadth and 49cm in width. The stone, which is roughly triangular in section, is aligned northeast-southwest and is separated by a distance of 92cm from stone 2, which lies to the southwest.  Stone 2 measures 80cm in height, 84cm in breadth and 59cm in width. The stone is aligned east west and is somewhat irregular in outline. A distance of 1.3m separates it from stone 3 which lies to the northwest.  Stone 3 measures 95cm in height, 79cm in breadth and c. 48cm in width. The stone, which tapers towards its north-west end, is aligned southeast-northwest. A distance of 45cm separates it from stone 4, which lies to the north of it.  Stone 4 is prostrate, measuring 1.05m in length, 46cm in breadth and 40cm in width. Stones 1 to 4 enclose an area roughly 3m north-south and 2.6m east-west.  The outlier, stone 5, stands c. 2m southwest of stone 3.  It measures 1.25 in height, 96cm in breadth and c. 59cm in width. The stone, which is rectangular in section, is aligned east west. A number of other stones lie scattered in and around the site and probably represent field clearance'.
See attached photograph and sketch plan drawn by the Castleisland District Archaeological Survey
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien
Date of upload: 21 April 2022

KE049-108----:
Stone row described by O'Hare (1996, 10) as consisting of; 'three stones, one of which is lying prostrate. A short distance west of the monument, the field of pasture in which it stands, slopes away to the north, south and west. The site commands a fine view over the Paps Mountains to the south. In the distance Carrauntoohil is visible to the southwest. Currow hill rises to the northwest, while further hills and valleys lie to the north and northeast.  The alignment has an overall length of c. 8.3m, and runs in a northeast-southwest direction.  Stone 1, which stands at the northeast end of the alignment, consists of a sandstone block. It measures 1.5Sm in height, 1.05 in breadth and 72cm in width.  A field fence has been built against the east face of the stone, while a drain has been dug around its base.  Stone 2, also of sandstone, stands 1.8m to the southwest of stone 1. It measures 1.55m in height, c. 1m in breadth and c. 80cm in width.  The prostrate stone 3 lies at a distance of 2.5m to the southwest of stone 2. The surface of this stone is noticeably cracked and brittle. According to the landowner, a fire was once set upon it, in an effort to break the stone up. Consisting of a calcareous sandstone containing a quartz vein, the stone measures 2.45m in length, and 1.70m in width. It is 62cm thick'.
See attached plan and elevation drawings of stone row taken from O'Hare 1996
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien
Date of upload: 21 April 2022
KE049-110----:
Possible stone circle described by O'Hare (1996, 11) as follows; 'The minutes of the Kerry Field Club record the presence of a number of "gallauns" "some overturned" in the townland of Ballahantouragh,  "these they identified as a stone circle with two large gallauns standing apart; one to the east and one to the west".  The site was disturbed and the stones were overturned by people searching for gold (Vol. 1, 1941, 180). Unfortunately the exact location of the site was not recorded in the above extract. However, its probable location was indicated to the author in April 1990, by the owner of this land. He recalled having seen one large stone at this site, to the east of which stood six or seven smaller stones in a circle. Today a stone, measuring 1.65m in height, c 1.40m in breadth and 80cm in width, stands at the site. It is bordered on the south by a field fence, running roughly southeast northwest. The stone, which is of sandstone, is roughly triangular in section and aligned east-west. The 2m gap which lies between the stone and the field fence, is occupied by stones which have obviously been cleared from elsewhere and just thrown there. A further jumble of stones lie at a distance of 28m roughly to the east of this stone. It is not possible to say whether or not these stones once formed a part of the monument or are merely stones gathered together in the course of field clearance. However, standing 2m to the south of these is another stone, roughly square in section and measuring 70cm in height, 75cm in breadth and 60cm in width. It consists of sandstone.  The field is under pasture, and in the general site area, slopes away to both the north and south, with a less obvious slope to the east. The site commands a view over the hillslope lying to the northwest, north and south, while the Paps mountains are visible in the distance to the southeast'.  Two upright stones are clearly visible on Digital Globe orthoimage taken between 2011-13.  These stones are clearly visible on Google Earth orthophoto taken 03/04/2013.
See attached Google Earth orthoimage.
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien
Date of upload: 21 April 2022

KE052-016----:
This monument is situated on the NW slope and close to the floor of the valley between Mount Eagle and Croaghmarhin. The structure, which is partly set into the slope and apparently much concealed, can be interpreted as the remains of a wedge-tomb. A single stone to the NE and 3 others along the SW side probably represent outer-walling. An upright stone to the NW and a fallen stone close by to the SW may be the remains of a facade. Some of the many slabs which litter the enveloping mound may once have formed part of the tomb; others are undoubtedly the result of field clearance.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 31. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 3 August 2013

Situated near the foot of the NW slope of Mount Eagle, this ruined monument is incorporated in a townland boundary fence which forms the N side of a disused laneway. It is known locally as Leac na mBuachaillí mBána. Two roofstones are partly embedded in the fence with that to the W supported by a single sidestone. Several stones are exposed in the S face of the fence but their relationship to the monument is uncertain. The monument is clearly a megalithic tomb but the remains are insufficient to allow classification.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 38. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE054-016----:
Situated on a generally W facing slope, commanding an extensive view over the Lispole valley and as far W as the Blasket Islands, this site is comprised of an alignment of 3 stones, 7.55m long, with an outlier standing 60m to NE.
The tallest stone, at the NE end of the line, stands 3m high and measures 1.7m x .4m at base. The middle stone, 1.38m further SW, is 2.2m high and 1.1m x .4m at base. The 3rd stone, 1.65m to SW again, is almost level with its neighbour and measures 1.3m x .5m at base. The alignment is orientated on the setting sun at the Winter Solstice (Lynch 1981b, 26).
The outlier stands 2.9m high and measures 2m x .58m at base; ENE-WSW. Its NW face bears a series of rock art motifs including a cup-and-2 circles centrally positioned on the face; below this are 2 cup-and-circles, and grouped together at the base of the stone are 2 cup-and-circles with radial lines, and a cup-and-incomplete circle. In addition there are 7 plain cup-marks and a series of linear grooves (the dotted lines on the drawing represent uncertain markings).
Immediately NW of this stone, a large boulder resting on 3 smaller ones was removed to make way for a track (local information). Based on the description and the context it is suggested that this feature was a boulder-dolmen; it is not unusual for such monuments to occur in close proximity to isolated or pairs of standing stones, although none have previously been recorded in association with a stone alignment (Ó Nualláin 1978a, 75-114).
See attached screenshots of 3D model of the rock art panel created by The Discovery Programme.  3D model can be accessed at the following website: https://skfb.ly/XQv9
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 50. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 3 August 2013

Pookauncorrin/Púicín an Chairn: This wedge-tomb is located near the E end of a long mountain ridge, overlooking Minard Bay on the S side of the Dingle peninsula. It commands an extensive outlook across Dingle Bay to the mountains of the Iveragh peninsula.
The monument, which stands at the junction of 3 stone fences, is in a good state of preservation but has been modified for use as an animal shelter. It consists of a wedge-shaped gallery incorporated in a mound of stones measuring 8m E-W and 5m N-S. The mound reaches to the level of the roof of the gallery but it is not clear to what extent it represents the original cairn. A stone at the E edge of the mound and a 2nd stone immediately within the perimeter at NW are well set in the ground and may be kerb-stones. The gallery, which at present measures 3.85m in length, decreases in height and width from W to E. It is 1.7m wide and 1.5m high at W and .9m wide and .75m high at E. The backstone is missing but has been replaced by a later stone wall. The entrance at W has also been closed by secondary walling. The N side of the gallery is represented by 4 orthostats. A gap of .9m between the 2 westernmost stones now provides access to the interior but probably originally contained a 5th orthostat. A single stone outside the wall, towards its E end, forms a doubling of the wall here. The S side of the gallery also consists of 4 orthostats. The structure is roofed by 2 slabs, that to W being supported partly by the side walls and partly by the E roof stone.
The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 34. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)

KE067-020002-:
In undulating pasture, with views W to Killarney and Macgillycuddy's Reeks. This stone circle (int. diam. c. 4m) lies in the centre of an earthen enclosure (int. diam. c. 20m) (KE067-020001-). The stone circle, which is comprised of seven stones (L 0.5-1.2m; T 0.4-1m; H 0.9-1.2m), was regarded by Ó Nualláin (1984a, 25, no. 38) as typical of the Cork-Kerry series, with the stones decreasing in height as they appraoch the axial stone at SW. A recent interpretation by O'Brien (2004, 329), however, concluded that the identification of the axial stone and the associated orientation are open to question. The enclosure is defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3.4m; int. H 1m; ext. H 0.8m), partially obscured by trees and bushes, and has breaks at NE and SW. A limited excavation in 1998 revealed the presence of a steep-sided fosse (Wth 3m at top, 1m at base; D 2.5m) directly inside the enclosing bank and also confirmed that the enclosure (KE067-020001-) is prehistoric in date (O'Brien 2000, 94-5; 2004, 323-38). A standing stone-pair (KE067-020004-) is c. 14m to the S.
Compiled by: Elizabeth Byrne, Ursula Egan and Sheila Ronan, Archaeological Survey Unit, University College, Cork.
Date of upload: 31 January 2011

KE068-022002-:
Near the centre of a cashel (KE068-022001-) named 'Cathair Craobh Dearg' and known locally as 'The City'. A stone (dims. 1.25m x 0.45m; H 0.95m) orientated NNW-SSE which was named 'Cromlech' on both the 1846 and 1894 OS 6-inch maps. KE070-016----:
This monument is located on a level shoulder of rough mountain pasture, on the lower S facing slope of Knocknadobar. There is a commanding view from the site to W, over the estuary of the Ferta river. The tomb is quite well-preserved, consisting of a gallery, open at both ends, with one cap-stone still in situ. It is orientated ENE-WSW and its sides are reinforced by low buttress-stones, set immediately outside. Traces of a low cairn are discernible, particularly on its S side. In the 1930s a separate rear chamber was noted at its E end (NMI).
The N side of the 4m long gallery is composed of three stones ranging in height from .7m to .38m; each is set inside the line of the forerunner to W. Four slabs represent the S side, the tallest, at W, standing .77m high; the remainder generally decrease in height towards the rear of the gallery at E. The width of the gallery decreases from 1.5m at W to just under 1m at the E end. Lines of external buttress-stones are set immediately against the side-stones of the gallery; four low orthostats occur on the N side, averaging .3m high and .35m wide, and eight similar slabs are visible on the S side, some of which are embedded in what appears to be cairn material. The cap-stone, located towards the E end of the gallery, rests directly on pad-stones and its ends oversail the sides of the chamber. It is irregularly shaped and measures 2.9m x 1.4m and .15m in average thickness. On its upper surface lies a .35m thick deposit of peaty material. Four other possible roof-stones lie in the immediate vicinity of the site; one occurs within the gallery. These may have been displaced when the tomb was partially dismantled, early in the twentieth century, to free a trapped farm animal (NMI).
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 72. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE070-035----:
Located on a ridge of rough grazing land, on the N side of the valley between Been Hill and Teermoyle mountain, this well-preserved wedge-tomb commands an extensive outlook to SW along the valley of the Ferta river. The monument, modified for use as an animal shelter, consists of a wedge-shaped gallery, 3.7m in overall length, and is aligned ENE-WSW. It is 1.2m wide and 1.05m high at its W end, and decreases in width and height at E to 1.1m and .75m respectively. Two orthostats represent the N side of the gallery, while three occur on the S side; both sides decrease in height from W to E. The back-stone is set outside the lends of the gallery walls. Two large flat roof-stones complete the chamber (de Valera and Ó Nuallain 1982, 61). The 'cupmarks', noted by Lynch on the upper surface of the roof-stones (1906a, 280-1), are probably solution pits. The stone at W collapsed into the gallery in 1992.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 73. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

The S side consists of three stones; the stone at W is set outside the line of the other two and may have served as a doubling to a now missing side-stone. A buttress-stone leans against it at W. The levels of the side-stones indicate a general decrease in height from W to E. A prostrate stone at the open W end of the gallery may represent a fallen septal- or door-stone (de Valera and Ó Nuallain 1982, 60).

This well-preserved wedge-tomb is situated on a level terrace, towards the end of an elevated ridge which extends SW from Feaghmann mountain, Valencia Island. The site commands an extensive view of the Portmagee Channel to S. The monument consists of a short, unusually broad chamber covered by a single roof-stone. It is aligned ENE-WSW and is set in a low mound which rises to a height of .5m at W. The chamber measures 3.5m long, 2m wide, and decreases from 1.25m in height at W to 1.1m at E. The sides of the tomb are each formed of a single slab, though a small orthostat is set inside the N side-stone at its E end. The roof-stone rests on all three stones and on a pad-stone. Leaning against the W end of the structure are three slabs, and another three slabs block its E end. None of the slabs appear to be original and they may have been employed to facilitate the use of the tomb as an animal shelter (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 61-2). Local tradition suggests that the monument was altered for use as a shelter by an evicted family in the nineteenth century.

The upright, 1.02m high, stands on edge N of the other stones and measures 2.4m x .16m at base; it is aligned NE-SW. Its upper edge slopes downwards from W to E and it appears to be a gallery side-stone. Lying .3m S of it, the first prostrate slab measures 2m x 1.82m x .15m; at least nine solution pits occur on its upper surface. It probably served as a roof-stone. The second slab lies adjacent to this at S and measures 2.37m x 1.28m x .1m; it may represent a gallery side-stone. According to local information, the wedge tomb was removed sometime around 2005 and the orthostats and roof-stone were deposited against a field boundary c. 200m to the east (ITM E 440384 N 576183).

Extending W from the base of the larger standing stone is a roughly rectangular stony area, measuring 11m x 6.5m. Large boulders, small stones and some uprights comprise this spread, which is delimited on its SE side by a low, curved, stone and earth bank. About 17m E of the standing stone is an L-shaped low bank, measuring 22.5m N-S and 23m E-W. Composed of stone and earth, the bank barely rises above the surrounding ground level and a scattering of boulders occurs along its length.

Deeply buried in rough boggy ground, this fairly well-preserved wedge-tomb is located on a small platform on the N side of the valley between Bentee and Aghatubrid mountains. It commands a wide outlook to W, over the basin of the Oghermong river to Valencia Island and the sea beyond. The field in which it is located is known locally as 'Gortaleaca'.
It consists of a chamber, roofed with two slabs, with the remains of aportico at its W end. Faint traces of a mound are visible on its S side. The chamber measures at least 2.9m in overall length and is aligned ENE-WSW. A markedly inclined septal-stone and an orthostat representing the N side of the portico are exposed at its W end. Two orthostats, decreasing in height towards E, form the S side of the chamber, while a collapsed side-stone is partly visible at N. Resting on the septal-stone is the high-pitched W roof-stone; it is slightly displaced and its E end is concealed by an overgrowth of peat which also overlies the adjacent E roof-stone.

KE082-007001-:
This site is situated in reclaimed bogland on the floor of the Bridia valley, 75m S of the Caragh river. The location is encircled by high mountains, except where the valley opens to W. Ó Nualláin recorded a possible boulder-burial NE of the site (1988, 239), but the land here was deep-ploughed in 1989 and no trace of this feature survives.
The stone row consists of three orthostats, the smallest of which was levelled in 1989. The other two stand in a ENE-WSW line, 2.25m apart. The taller stone, at ENE, is of trapezoidal plan at base and of somewhat irregular elevation; it stands 2.27m high and has maximum dimensions of .87m x .33m at base. The second stone tapers in elevation towards a flat top, rising to a height of 1.88m; it measures .57 x .46m at base. The third component of the row was a low stone which stood c. 1.2m further to WSW; it measured .4m high and .58m x .3m at base. Analysing the significance of this monument's orientation, Lynch concluded that it was aligned on the rising sun at the summer solstice (1981b, 26).
The possible boulder-burial was located 24m to the NE of the stone row. Before destruction it comprised a large boulder, 1.6m x 1.35m, which rested above four or more small stones (Ó Nuallain 1988, 238-9, Fig. 14).
The stone row was disturbed during land reclamation operations in 1989 and, as a result, was excavated (Sheehan 1990a, 30). The socket of the felled orthostat and the area around the two remaining uprights were investigated. A shallow pit and a number of stake-holes were discovered close to the ENE orthostat, but these may not be contemporary with the monument. The location of the possible boulder-burial was also excavated, but no finds or features were noted.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 108. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE085-001----:
In rough boggy pasture, on a plateau broken by rock outcrops at the W end of the Derrynasaggart Mountains. The wedge tomb is partially hidden in bog. It consists of an unroofed antechamber (L 1.1m; Wth 1.3m) of single sidestones at the W end, which is separated from the chamber (L 1.55m; Wth 1m) by a pair of jambs (L 0.3m), 0.9m apart. The chamber is roofed by a single slab carried on two sidestones at each side. A single stone closes the E end, which is covered by peat. Two slabs beyond the S side of the antechamber represent outer-walling. Two large leaning slabs cross the W end of the structure and between these is a tall slender stone (L 0.45m; T 0.15m; H 1.3m). A loose displaced stone (L 1.55m; Wth 0.9m; T 0.15m) stands on edge behind the facade. This may have formed part of the roof. The tomb is surrounded by a small mound (H 0.5m). (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, no. 14, 63-4)
Compiled by: Elizabeth Byrne, Ursula Egan and Sheila Ronan, Archaeological Survey Unit, University College, Cork.
Date of upload: 31 January 2011

KE085-053001-:
Possible megalithic tomb identified by Miriam Carroll, Tobar Archaeological Services following monitoring of a wind farm at Lettercannon, Co. Kerry 17 February 2009.  Two possible sites, located within 5m of each other, which were described as comprising 'of a possible stone hut site and a possible ruinous megalithic tomb, the latter is a very tentative suggestion'. Both are located within a windfarm (under construction) but are fenced off.  Monuments described by Miriam Carroll as; 'The site consists of a stone feature in a small clearing surrounded by coniferous trees. It is comprised of three large stones situated on a low rise and was somewhat obscured by vegetation, The upper stone measures approximately 3m in length and rests on two underlying stones of similar length which may have fallen from an upright position. The precise nature of the site is unclear but may represent the remains of a small megalithic tomb.'
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien based on details provided by Miriam Carroll
Date of upload: 27 September 2022

A possible ‘gallaun’, which is not marked on the OS maps, apparently stood at this location before its removal in the 1930s. It was described as standing over six feet (1.8m) high, and an iron ‘spearhead’ was reported to have been found during its removal (local information). The monument stood at the foot of the steep N slopes of Bray Head, and overlooked Emlagh bog and the Atlantic beyond. Some local reports suggest that it bore an ogham inscription.

KE088-032----:
This site, which abuts the W end of an area of rock outcrop, occurs on S sloping pastureland and overlooks the estuary of the Inny river. Close by, at S, is a children's burial ground (KE088-033----). The monument is well-preserved and survives as a chamber, open to SW, covered by a single roof-stone. Traces of a cairn are apparent on the N side of the structure, which is formed by a single slab measuring .65m high, 2.82m long and averaging .25m thick. It inclines slightly inwards. The opposite side of the chamber is formed by two orthostats, both of regular elevation. They stand an average of .75m high and measure .7m x .2m at base. The irregularly shaped roof-stone is supported on its NE side on natural rock outcrop, and measures 1.53m x 1m x .16m. A low section of drystone walling is visible at the rear of the chamber, which is wedge-shaped and decreases in height and width from SW to NE. It is 1m high and 1.15m wide at SW, and .76m high and .97m wide at NE.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 88. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 28 July 2013
KE088-039----:
Located on the S side of a ridge which runs E from Fermoyle mountain, this site commands an extensive outlook to S over Ballinskelligs Bay. The monument is poorly preserved and comprises a single large roof-stone, which overlies a number of collapsed side-stones. The longer axis of the roof-stone, which tilts downwards towards E, lies ENE-WSW. Irregular in plan, it measures 2.85m x 2.07m x .35m. A number of solution pits occur on its upper surface. Three partly visible slabs protrude from beneath this stone. The first, which may represent a collapsed N side-stone, is at least 1.2m long. The second, measuring 1.9m x 1.2m x .2m, may represent a collapsed S side-stone, while the third, a small block measuring .4m x .3m x .1m, located adjacent to the N side-stone, may have functioned as a pad-stone. A quantity of small stones, including some quartz, occurs beneath the roof-stone and may represent field clearance.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 87. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE089-015----:
Located on the N side of a boggy ridge on the lower S slopes of Aghatubrid mountain, this megalithic tomb abuts a large area of rock outcrop titled 'Carrigaphuca' on the OS maps. It consists of a chamber, open to NW, and is covered by a single roof-stone. It is deeply buried in the boggy ground and its interior is frequently waterlogged. The NE side of the chamber is formed by two orthostats; that at SE is the larger and is .65m high, 1.55m long and .15m thick. A low orthostat occurs at right angles to the second side-stone and partly closes the chamber. A large, outwardly inclining slab forms the SW side; this is 1.8m long, c .5m thick and, if erect, would be c .75m high. One large slab forms the skewed rear of the chamber; it is .6m high, 1.62m long and .18m thick. The large, irregularly shaped cap-stone rests on the end-stone and on the two side-stones; it is 2m long, 2.5m wide and .35m in maximum thickness. A number of pre-bog walls occur in the immediate vicinity of the site. One runs the length of the entire slope, breaking only at the location of the tomb. Many of the walls have collapsed, but in general they survive up to 1m above the level of the bog.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 89. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 28 July 2013

KE089-031----:
This stone row is situated on a plateau on the NW slopes of Coomduff ridge, overlooking the Inny river. The tallest standing stone on the peninsula is located 150m to E (KE089-033----). The 8.3m long row consists of three stones, orientated NE-SW, with an outlying monolith 15.5m to SW. The stories of the row decrease in size from NE to SW. The tallest measures 1.9m x 1.4m x .6m and inclines slightly to SE. The second stands 1.2m to SW, and measures 1.2m x .9m x .4m; it inclines towards NW. The third and shortest stone stands 3.8m further to SW, and measures .7m x .5m x .35m. A prostrate slab, 7.6m to S, is largely buried in the ground and its relationship to the row is unclear. The outlier at SW is set roughly in line with the stone row and measures 1.55m x .7m x .6m; packing stones are exposed at its base (Ó Nuallain 1988, 239).
Analysing the significance of this monument's orientation, Lynch concluded that it was aligned to W on the S limit of the major lunar standstill (1981b, 26).
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 105. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 28 July 2013

KE089-035----:
Located on the SE side of Coomduff and overlooking the Cummeragh river, this site consists of a row of three stones incorporated into a low cairn. The row is oriented NE-SW and is c. 7m long. The stone at NE is 1.7m high and measures .7m x .65m at base. The second stone, appreciably taller, stands 1.75m to SW; it is 3.3m high and measures .95m x .75m at base. The third stone stands on edge 2.2m further to SW; measuring 2.5m x 1m, it stood in an upright position up to the 1930s (local information).
The cairn consists of a platform-like terrace of stone and measures 7.6m long and up to 1m high above the ground level on its SE side. A quantity of quartz is evident in its composition. The landowner indicated that the cairn was originally larger, and that it was faced on its downslope side. O'Connell reported that a 'bronze staff was found in it (1939a, 31), but the present location of this object is unknown. The site is locally referred to as the 'Cloughane'.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 107. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 28 July 2013

It is visibly weathered on the S face, and one packing stone is evident at its base.

KE089-042----:
Marked 'Gallaun' on the OS maps, this site is situated in boggy pasture, on the SE slopes of Coomduff, and overlooks the valley of the Cummeragh river. It consists of three stones, orientated NE-SW, the easternmost lying prostrate and measuring 2.45m x 1.05m x .25m.
