KE091-121----:
Situated in boggy pasture, in a clearing partially enclosed by trees.. A stone circle (diam. 8.5–9m) composed of 8 stones (H: c.0.4–1.2m), the highest of which is located at N. Each of the stones is lichen encrusted on all sides which suggests the stones have been in their current positions for a long period of time. Packing stones are not visible. This stone circle is not characteristic of the multiple stone circles of Cork and Kerry in that it is composed of an even rather than an uneven number of stones and does not have a recumbent stone at SW. A fire setting in the centre of the stone circle appears modern. Immediately S of the circle is a low heap of modern field clearance material consisting of loose boulders and vegetation. A table-top boulder directly S of this heap has possibly been recently placed in this position as it is largely devoid of lichen encrustation and bears marks which appear to be machine lacerations. A semi-derelict house which is unoccupied is within sight of the stone circle 55m to SSE. Expansive views are afforded from the stone circle towards Mullaghanattin at N and NE. Due to modern dykes and ditches around the the circle as well as forestry and other vegetation, the circle itself is largely obscured from view other than from within close range.  A kerb circle in Gortacloghane (KE091-
015001) is located 2.1km to ENE.

KE092-001----:
This severely disturbed site is depicted as two standing-stones, titled 'Gallauns', on the first edition of the OS map. It is recorded in the OSNB as 'two tall stones about 4 feet asunder' which were each '7 feet over the surface and 3 1/2 feet thick' (Templeno, 16). The site is located in rough pasture, a short distance N of the Derreendarragh river, and now consists of an earth and stone mound with a large prostrate slab on its surface. The low, flat-topped mound is of subcircular plan and measures 25m in overall diameter. The slab, partially concealed beneath a holly tree, is rectangular in outline. It features a straight edge at its present E end, while its W end tapers to a rounded point. It measures 3m long, 1.1m wide and .4m thick. There is no apparent trace of the second stone.
Windele assigned this site to an incorrect townland (Derreendarragh) and recorded that, several months before his visit to it in 1848, the standing stones had been undermined by 'treasure seekers' and toppled one over the other. He noted that the uppermost stone bore an ogham inscription, and that both had formerly stood within a barely perceptible 'circle of stones' which had a diameter of 33 feet (10.1m). This circle was comprised of fifteen or sixteen stones (RIA MS 12 C 11). Brash visited the site in 1872, by which time half of the mound had been cut away and a number of the stones, which he described as having formed a 'megalithic sepulchral arrangement' around the prostrate slabs, had been removed. The ogham stone was damaged, and a large flake had been knocked off its inscribed angle. It measured 10 feet (3.04m) long, 3 feet 6 inches (1.06m) wide and 2 feet 10 inches (.86m) thick, and the inscription was cut in deep, broad grooves (1879, 192-5). Both Windele and Brash read it as:
ANM CRUNAN MAQ LUQISMA
Macalister recorded that the site was demolished by road-makers in the late 1880s (1945, 213-4). He accepted Hitchcock's illustration (RIA MS 24 E 39) of the ogham inscription, which gives a similar reading to Windele's and Brash's except that it ends with LUQIN.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 128. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE094-095----:
New site identified by John Cronin & Associates (JCA) under Licence No. 16E0127 prior to wind farm development in Barnastooka, Kilgarvan, Co. Kerry by ESB Wind Development Ltd.  Located on a level terrace in rough boggy pasture, mid-slope on the north-western side of upper reaches of a valley which contains a tributary of the Roughty River, the remains of a wedge-shaped gallery aligned east to west. Most prominent upstanding remains are those of the sidestones of the chamber along the northern side of the tomb (three sidestones upstanding, largest to west), evidence of double walling with internal packing along northern side. Southern sidestones (excluding one small upstanding sidestone near entrance) have collapsed inwards under the weight of two large capstones. At entrance to gallery on west side, two upright stones which lean inwards towards each other (southern stone leaning on northern stone) may be the remains of a portico. A vertical slab, set at surface level on its long axis and located immediately behind the possible portico, may be a septal stone, separates the entrance from the main chamber. Maximum dimensions of upstanding remains measure 4.68m in length (E-W), 2.40m in width (N-S), 1.32m in height. Maximum length of feature as measured from eastern end of largest collapsed roofstone (L. 2.78m E-W, W. 2.14m N-S, T 0.2m) which lies off-centre to southeast is 5.05m. Details on eastern and south-eastern sides masked by the collapsed large roofstone. The smaller probable roofstone (also collapsed but in a more central position) is perforated by two 50mm diameter holes, spaced 0.7m apart, partial perforation attempt also evident immediately east of western hole. Evidence of outer cairn surrounding the chamber, particularly at north and west sides, probable kerbing stones evident 1.9m north of northern upstanding sidestones of chamber. Burial cairn (NICH22) is located c.100m downslope to the east.
See attached photograph courtesy John Cronin.
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien based on details provided by John Cronin

This poorly preserved megalithic chamber is situated on the S side of a low ridge which overlooks Ballinskelligs Bay to S. Three orthostats survive in situ; two form an angled W side to the chamber, while the third, at N, may be an end-stone. Three prostrate slabs nearby may represent E side-stones and a roof-stone. Traces of an oval cairn surround the structure, though the rubble fill within the chamber appears to be modern field clearance. The S stone on the W side of the chamber is .96m long, .32m thick and .67m high. The N stone on this side is 1.02m long, .38m thick and .8m high. The stone at the N end of the monument, disposed at right angles to the latter, is regular in elevation and is partly concealed. It is at least 1m long, and measures .44m thick and .45m high. The stones which formed the E side of the chamber have collapsed inwardly and are largely covered in sod. A displaced slab which lies within the chamber may have originally served as a roof-stone. This measures 1.2m long by .6m wide.

This monument is located in reclaimed bogland near the head of a valley that opens E to Ballinskelligs Bay. The gallery, aligned NE-SW, consists of a wedge-shaped chamber, covered by a single roof-stone, and a parallel-sided portico to W. Excavation revealed the scant remains of a trapezoidal cairn, 12m long and narrowing from 10m wide at W to c. 2m at E, which was revetted by a row of small upright stones. The cairn had been largely removed before the commencement of peat growth. A flint flake with secondary working along one edge was found beneath it, but no definite evidence of burial was found in the chamber (Herity 1966, 67).
The main chamber is 2.85m long and tapers sharply from a width of 1.45m at W to .4m at E. The chamber is closed at E by one slab, set outside the ends of the side-walls. Each side-wall consists of one long and one short stone. A blocking stone divides the portico from the main chamber. The roof-stone, 3.2m long, rests on the side-stones in an inclined position. Excavation showed that the portico consisted of three stones on either side; originally it may have been roofed by a slab resting in an inclined position with its lower end on the chamber roof-stone. The portico measures 2.3m long and 1.45m wide. The overall internal length of the gallery is 5.45m (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 65).

National Monument No. 380.   This boulder-burial and standing stone are located in gently sloping pasture close to the W shores of Lough Currane. A second standing stone (KE098-034----) occurs c. 167m to SSW. The boulder-burial consists of a flat-topped slab supported on three low stones. The interior of the monument is infilled with field debris, and larger clearance stones abut it externally at E and W. The cover-stone is roughly subrectangular in plan, its longer axis lying ENE-WSW. Its maximum dimensions are 1.8m x 1.5m and it averages .3m thick. The support stones are generally flat-topped and have average dimensions of .7m x .5m and .3m high. In 1988 a single piece of burnt bone was found beneath the cover-stone (NMI 1988:190).
Located 13.4m ENE of the boulder-burial is a stout pillar (KE098-030002-) of regular elevation, marked 'Gallaun' on the OS maps. Its NE side displays a sharp inturn 1.45m up from its base, where it measures 1.05m x .8m; ENE-WSW. The stone stands 2.4m high and a number of packing stones are exposed at its base (Ó Nualláin 1978, 98).
Henry noted two small 'dolmens' to the W of the standing stone, where she also recorded the ruins of one or two huts and related field boundaries (1957, 132). No visible trace survives of this second possible boulder-burial, nor of the other features.

This four-stone row is situated in a prominent position on the crest of a ridge running between Lough Currane and Ballinskelligs Bay, and commands extensive views in all directions. The field in which the site is located has recently been reclaimed, and an enclosure incorporates the monument on its NW side. The stone row is aligned ENE-WSW and is 8.6m long. The orthostat at ENE inclines heavily to N, and measures 1.7m x 1.55m x .3m; between it and the second stone is a prostrate slab. The second stone, 1.28m to WSW, stands 1.9m high and measures .85m x .65m at base. Disposed at right angles to its SE face is a slab set on edge which measures .88m high, 1.17m wide and .25m thick. The third stone, .95m to WSW, stands 2.72m high and measures 1.52m x .52m at base. A further .5m to WSW is the fourth stone, which is irregular in elevation, particularly along its NE edge; it stands 2.8m high and its basal dimensions are 2.1m x .32m. Lying against its SE face is a large slab, the function of which is unclear. The remains of an old wall occur between the orthostats and spill downslope to NW.
Analysing the significance of the stone row's orientation, Lynch concluded that it was aligned on the setting sun at the winter solstice (1981b, 26). Ó Nualláin, however, expressed doubt about the status of this monument because of its location on the perimeter of the enclosure (1988, 200). It is reputed to mark the burial place of Sceine, the wife of Amergin, the Milesian leader (Barrington 1976, 284).
The enclosure, suboval in plan, incorporates the stone row on its NW side. Internally it measures 15.5m NW-SE x 13.8m NE-SW. The bank, which has been greatly denuded since Lynch's description of it (1902b, 331), appears to be composed of earth intermixed with stone. It is 1.3m high externally at W, and its top is almost flush with the interior. Lynch excavated a portion of it and found it to be constructed of stone; he recorded it as four feet (1.2m) wide and three feet (.9m) high (1902b, 331). A 1m wide entrance-like gap occurs at E and is flanked on its N side by a large upright, 1.12m high. A slab set on edge defines its S side. Two other slabs lying nearby may have formed part of the entrance.

The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 132. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 28 July 2013
KE099-018001-:
This site is located on the crest of a NE-SW ridge which is flanked on W and S by the Bunnow river and overlooks Kenmare Bay to S. It consists of a three-stone row, 5.1m to NE of which is an enclosure. The stone row is 3.1m long and is orientated NE-SW. The stone at NE stands 1.7m high, inclines slightly to SW, and measures .45m x .2m at base. The second stone, .45m to the SW, leans heavily to NW; it measures 1.3m x .54m x .3m. A large prostrate stone, 2.35m x .6m x .4m, lies 1.05m to SW. When erect, it may have been the tallest stone in the row.
The adjacent enclosure may be a kerb circle, as defined by Lynch (1979, 2). It is a roughly circular area, 7.25m N-S x 6.7m E-W, which is delineated by a kerb of contiguous upright slabs enclosing a low pile of boulders, small stones and quartz. The orthostats, many of which incline outwardly, average .9m high and .8m x .2m at base. A field boundary incorporates some of the slabs at SW, and a gap at NW is obscured by overgrowth. The enclosure is marked 'Killeen Burial Ground' on both editions of the OS maps.
It is locally reputed that a rock with 'ancient writing' is located in the vicinity of the stone row. A search for this potential monument proved unsuccessful
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 101. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 28 July 2013
KE099-025----:
This standing stone is described in the OSNB as having been ‘lately thrown down by a treasure seeker’ (Kilcrohane, 27). Not marked on the OS maps, it was located on top of a ridge, in an area surrounded by bog. Its siting commanded a panoramic view across the neighbouring low-lying land. Part of the stone survived up to the 1950s, (local information), but is no longer visible.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 238. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE101-007001-:
In the garden of a house, to the N of the Kenmare-Castletownbere road and c. 9.5km SW of Kenmare. In 1841 this stone circle was described as 'a circle of standing stones with a small cromlech [KE101-007002-] in the centre. The circle is thirty-five feet, six inches [10.82m] in diameter and composed of twelve standing stones, each being from four feet to five feet ten inches [1.21m-1.77m] in height, three feet [0.91m] wide and two feet [0.6m] thick' (OSL, 176). According to Ó Nualláin (1984a, 28, no. 44), the stone circle was in a ruinous condition for many years and was reconstructed c. 1964 and most likely now bears little resemblance to its original form. It now consists of a U-shaped arrangement of loosely set upright stones with a possible boulder-burial (KE101-007002-) in the centre.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Kerry. Volume I: South-West Kerry' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 30 May 2011

The top flag is supported by three small stones not more than three feet [0.91m] in height; it measures six feet [1.82m] from East to West, five feet [1.52m] from North to South and is one foot, three inches [0.38m] in thickness' (OSL, 176). All that now remains of this possible boulder-burial is a flat slab (max. dim. 1.8m). (Ó Nualláin 1978, 98-9, no. 40).

KE101-010001-:
In rough pasture, on the W side of the valley of the Dromoghty River. This stone circle (diam. 9.5m) consists of thirteen stones (L 0.8-1.6m; T 0.3-0.6m; H 0.8-1.6m), three of which are prostrate. Only one entrance stone stands and it is radially set on the circumference at E. The axial stone has a flat top and, unusually, it is not the lowest stone in the circle. In the interior of the circle is a centrally placed boulder-burial (KE101-010002-) and 2m S of it is a standing stone (KE101-010003-). (Ó Nualláin 1971, fig. 2, site D; 1984a, 28-9, no. 45)

Small pad-stones on top of each support-stone serve to steady the boulder. A standing stone (KE101-010003-), also stands in the centre of the stone circle, 2m to the S of the boulder-burial. KE101-025001-:
In rough pasture, on the N slope of Knockreagh Mountain. An irregular circle (diam. 7.5m NE-SW x 8.5m NW-SE) of ten stones (H 1-1.25m; 0.6-1.4m x 0.4-0.7m), two of which have fallen and another two of which are incorporated into a field boundary at SW. A large gap between two stones in the SE arc suggests the former presence of an eleventh stone. Two transversely set entrance stones stand at NE and directly opposite is the flat-topped axial stone. Two low stones (H 0.3 and 0.4m) are exposed 2m NE of the entrance and may be an elaboration of this feature or perhaps part of a field boundary. A boulder-burial (KE101-025002-) occupies the centre of the circle and a possible fulacht fia (KE101-025004-) abuts the outer face of the axial stone. Three further boulder-burials (KE101-025003-, KE101-025005-, KE101-025006-) stand c. 8-10m to the SW. (Twohig 1987, 111-18)

KE104A001008-:
KE104A001008- The Spit: This feature comprises a short, narrow, steep-sided ridge which runs to E from just below the level of the summit of the S peak. It is c. 3m long and varies in width, narrowing to only 0.2m towards the middle. A broad, upright slab, c. 1m high, formerly stood at its E end; this fell in the late 1970s.
Described in 1990 as follows; 'The summit is small—a few rock ledges—and consists of the ultimate peak of the rock, crowned by a modern iron weathervane, and the Spit. Smith (1756, 115) noted that pilgrims called the summit "the eagle's nest, probably from its extreme height; for here, a person seems to have got into the superior region of the air." The Spit, a narrow ridge some two meters below the weathervane on the eastern side of the peak, was legendary. At its far end lay the goal of the pilgrims—the upright slab that had to be kissed. Most writers on the South Peak, from Smith in 1756 to Hayward in 1946, mentioned the slab. Sometime after 1977, however, it disappeared, probably falling from its base. No part has ever been found, and only traces of dry-stone masonry remain in the socket where the slab had been anchored by layered stone. Fortunately, archaeologists made photographs and took measurements of the slab in 1977.  The visible part of the slab was approximately 1 meter high and 7.6 centimeters thick. No design was engraved on it, but a tiny cross, barely perceptible, was scratched into the surface, perhaps by a pilgrim.  The Spit itself is roughly 3 meters long and varies in width, narrowing in the middle to only 0.2 meter. It is reached from a lower rock to its west, and it can be partly circumnavigated at its base on a campion-covered ledge. The Spit projects over the jagged valley hundreds of feet below. Stepping upon it is chilling; more commonly people sit and inch along its narrow downward-sloping surface.
There are no archaeological vestiges on the summit that we can relate with certainty to the hermitage. Although the slab at the end of the Spit may have been placed there by a hermit, it may also have been erected later by zealous pilgrims. The summit was surely important to the hermitage nonetheless, for to gain access to the outer terrace it was necessary first to climb almost to the summit' (Horn et. al. 1990, 53-4).
See attached figures 46 and 47 taken from Horn, W., White Marshall, J. and Rourke, G. 1990 The forgotten hermitage of Skellig Michael.
The above description is derived from A. O'Sullivan and J. Sheehan (compilers), 'The Iveragh peninsula: an archaeological survey of South Kerry'. Cork University Press (1996), no. 948. In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

KE106-036001-:
Coomatloukane townland, where four wedge-tombs occur is located on a steeply sloping SW spur of Farraniaragh mountain, close to the SW end of the peninsula. The land is characterised by rock outcrop and boulders, with intervening stretches of rough boggy pasture, and it affords broad views to S across the mouth of the Kenmare river to the Beara Peninsula. Much of the land has been reclaimed, though not in the vicinity of the wedge-tombs. The three northern tombs, which form a group (KE106-036001-, KE106-036002- and KE106-037----), were excavated by Herity (1967, 218).
The best preserved of these is situated on a small platform and consists of a narrow wedge-shaped gallery, aligned E-W, flanked on either side by outer-walling; single upright slabs link the ends of this walling to the front of the gallery. A prostrate stone found at the entrance may have segmented the 4m long gallery, which measures 1.05m wide at W and narrows to .7m at E. A shattered roof-stone covers the rear of the gallery, where the back-stone is missing. Loose cairn material extended beyond the limits of the outer walling (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 66). A small quantity of cremated bone was found in the gallery during its excavation.

KE107-019----:
Possible stone circle identified and described by Aoibheann Lambe as follows; 'Set on the grounds of a modern bungalow in an area that is overgrown, it is situated on a rise beyond the garden, with expansive views over the roof of the house at SE to Skehanagh and at SW to Kenmare River.  This possible stone circle is located on an overgrown elevated site in the townland of Liss and overlooks Kenmare River to SW. It consists of a circular arrangement of six upright stones and at least 7 more stones, one of which lies prostrate and others which have become obscured by the overgrowth or have been displaced by falling, particularly those on its south side where there is a drop of 1m at the edge of the circle. The level ground of the interior which has a diameter of 6m (6m NS and 6m EW) is overgrown and there are a number of young trees growing in it. The prostrate stone at NE is rectangular in shape and measures 1.25m by 0.6m and is 0.2m thick. At NNE, an upright stone, 1m high, 1.2m across at its widest point and 0.2m thick, tilts forward into the circle. Immediately in front of this is some rubble and a stone shaped like a triangular prism, the side facing the interior of the circle measuring 0.7m across at its base, its surface sloping upwards measuring 0.9m and the top surface 0.5m. Between N to NE, there is a gap c. 3m wide with an embankment, 0.2m high, extending to a field wall 7m to E. At ENE, there are two stones with the one nearest N being 0.45m high, 1.1m long at its base and 0.6m thick. The other is upright, standing 1.15m high, and is 1.5m wide and 0.4m thick. At ESE, a stone measuring 0.5m high on the side facing the circle and 1m on the other side, is 0.8m wide and 0.2m thick. At S, there is a stone 0.2m thick, 1m wide whose interior face is 0.35m high while the exterior face is 1m long. To S, there is a drop of 1m and it is very overgrown. There are at least 4 stones (c. 1m long) on the lower level that may have formed part of the circle. At W, there is a gap between 2 upright stones one 0.75m high, 0.75m wide and 0.4m thick while the other boulder is triangular shaped with the side facing the interior of the circle measuring 1m by 1m by 1m. There are 2 large boulders outside the circle, one 3m SW of this triangular shaped stone and the other a further 4m SW. Neither portals nor an axial stone have been identified'.

KE108-013001-:
In rough pasture, on a terrace to the S of a medieval road (KE108-013007-), on the lower N-facing slopes of Knocknaveacal. The remains of this stone circle comprised two upright stones (1.4m x 0.4m; H 2.55m; 0.9m x 0.7m; H 1.5m), 3.4m apart and between them a fallen stone resting against outcropping rock. The fallen stone was re-erected following on from the excavation in 1977 which revealed that the upright stones formed part of a circle (diam. c. 17m) of eleven or thirteen stones (Lynch 1981, 65-9). The only artifact recovered during the excavation was a flint scraper. A standing stone (KE108-013008-) which was indicated c. 30m NW of the stone circle on the 1897 OS 6-inch map, but which does not survive, may have been an outlier of this stone circle. A five-stone circle (KE108-013004-) and a stone row (KE108-013002-) lie c. 80m to the E and there are field boundaries (KE108-013005-) to the N and E. (Ó Nualláin 1984a, 29, no. 47)

KE108-022----:
In pasture, in the narrow valley of the Drimminboy River. An incomplete circle (diam. 7.5m) comprising eight upright stones (H 1.18-2m; 0.8-2m x 0.2-0.6m) and one fallen stone, stands in an arc ESE-NNW. One stone (H 0.4m) appears to be broken. The axial stone, which leans inwards, has a flat top and is the longest and lowest stone. The stones in the S half of the perimeter decrease in height as they approach the axial stone. Ó Nualláin (1984a, 29) suggests that this stone circle, 'if symmetrically designed, would seem to have consisted of thirteen closely-set stones'. (Ó Nualláin, 1984a, 29, no. 46)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Kerry. Volume I: South-West Kerry' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 30 May 2011

In rough pasture, on a ridge on the lower slopes of Knochanouganish Hill. This stone circle (diam. 8.5m) consists of nine pillar-like orthostats (L 0.35-1.3m; T 0.3-0.6m; H 1.15-2.1m). Two radially set stones form the entrance at NNE, the most easterly stone leaning to the W. The circle may originally have had eleven stones as the axial stone and one other stone are missing. A relict field boundary (KE109-003003-) lies c. 1m to the N. (Ó Nualláin 1984a, 30, no. 48)

In rough pasture, on a terrace on the N-facing slopes of Knockanouganish Hill. A well-preserved oval cairn (10m N-S; 7.75m E-W) encloses this wedge tomb. The chamber (L 1.5m; Wth 1.3m at the W end; Wth 0.93m at the E end), which is aligned E-W and open at W, is formed by a backstone and a single sidestone on each side. The roofstone (3.2m x 2.25m; T 0.3m) slopes down to the E and rests on the backstone and the N sidestone. The E half of the roofstone is covered by the cairn which has quartz inclusions. (Twohig 1986, 143-50)
